summary: Updates the use of the P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity SIP header fields from RFC 3325. It covers cases RFC 3325 did not, such as insertion by a trusted user agent client and use with methods like UPDATE and REGISTER. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It extends the rules for who may write the trusted this is really who is calling note on phone calls and in which situations.

questions: can a sip client send p-asserted-identity
subtitle: Lets trusted SIP clients assert identity and allows asserted identity on almost every SIP request.

tldr.problem: RFC 3325 let SIP servers in a trust domain assert who sent a request, but it did not cover a trusted client doing so, most request methods beyond INVITE, or unexpected URIs in the header.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5876 allows a trusted User Agent Client to add P-Asserted-Identity, allows P-Asserted-Identity and P-Preferred-Identity in any request except ACK and CANCEL, and says to ignore unexpected URIs.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3325 and is Informational. Asserted identity still works only inside a Trust Domain and is not specified for responses.

facts.label: URIs per header
facts.value: At most two (SIP or SIPS, plus TEL)

today: RFC 5876 is an Informational document that updates RFC 3325. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What RFC 3325 Left Open
sections.content:
RFC 3325 defines how the originator of a SIP request is identified within a Trust Domain, using the P-Asserted-Identity header field. A P-Preferred-Identity header field lets a client say which identity it would like asserted when it has a choice.

The gaps were these: no rule for a User Agent Client (UAC) in the same Trust Domain as the first proxy to insert P-Asserted-Identity; no rule for methods such as UPDATE, REGISTER, MESSAGE and PUBLISH; and no clear handling of an unexpected number or type of URIs. RFC 5876 fills these gaps. It does not change that asserted identity applies only within a Trust Domain. For identity beyond that, it points to the Identity header field of RFC 4474.
sections.eli5: An older rulebook said how a trusted switchboard could write down who was calling. This update covers a few cases the old book forgot.

sections.title: Why Allow More Methods and Senders
sections.content:
Types of UAC often suitable for a Trust Domain include PSTN gateways, media servers, and application servers that act as URI list servers or perform third party call control. A PSTN gateway may be able to assert an identity received from the PSTN, which the proxy itself cannot authenticate.

Use cases for other methods: a gateway can send an UPDATE with P-Asserted-Identity to announce that the remote party changed, for example after a call transfer, avoiding a re-INVITE that forces an offer-answer exchange and uses three messages rather than two. A back-to-back user agent joining two calls can use UPDATE to give early identity indications. REGISTER, MESSAGE and PUBLISH also benefit.

ACK and CANCEL are excluded because asserting an identity requires authenticating the sender, typically by challenging for SIP digest authentication, and ACK and CANCEL cannot be challenged. A P-Asserted-Identity in a request also says nothing about later requests in the same dialog.
sections.eli5: A trusted helper at the phone company boundary can now pass along who is calling, and can send a quick update when the person on the line changes. Messages that cannot be double-checked are left out.

sections.title: Behaviour of Each SIP Element
sections.content:
A UAC MAY include P-Asserted-Identity in any request except ACK and CANCEL, but SHOULD do so only when it believes it is in the same Trust Domain as the entity it sends to. A UAC SHOULD NOT do so otherwise, and might use P-Preferred-Identity instead. A UAC MUST NOT include both header fields.

A proxy receiving the header from a UAC in the Trust Domain MUST handle it as from any other trusted node, following RFC 3325, which implies it has authenticated the sender. A registrar MUST disregard an asserted identity in a REGISTER unless it comes from a node within the Trust Domain, and in that case MAY treat it as evidence the registering UA is authenticated. A User Agent Server MUST apply RFC 3325 rules even for methods RFC 3325 did not list.

For unexpected URIs, a receiver MUST ignore URIs with an unexpected scheme and URIs beyond the expected count. Unless a Spec(T) says otherwise, each header may hold at most two URIs: one SIP or SIPS and one TEL. A proxy MUST NOT forward a URI that is to be ignored. If a peer follows RFC 3325 but not this document and the request also has a Privacy header with value id, the peer may mishandle it, so the Spec(T) SHOULD require all nodes to comply.
sections.eli5: Each helper has a rule: trusted ones may write the note, everyone else must ignore notes from untrusted places, and extra or strange entries are thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A proxy trusts an assertion only if the source is known to be inside the Trust Domain and behaves according to its Spec(T). An entity adding P-Asserted-Identity must have authenticated the source, for example with SIP digest authentication. Responses cannot be challenged, so this document does not specify use of either header field in responses. A UA under an individual user's control, such as a desk phone or mobile phone, should typically not be considered part of a Trust Domain.
sections.eli5: You only believe the note if it comes from someone you already trust and can check. A person's own phone is not in that trusted group.
